one_liner: Small Metal GPU renderer for immediate-mode UIs (Apple only); its author reports 120 fps where nanovg managed 30 fps.
what_it_does: vger draws a fixed set of 2D primitives on Apple GPUs through Metal: circles, arcs, rounded rectangles (filled or stroked), line segments, wires, quadratic Bezier strokes, path fills built from quadratics, and CoreText text with solid, gradient, texture or grid paints. The drawing calls are a plain C API (vgerBegin, vgerFillRect, vgerStrokeBezier, vgerMoveTo/vgerQuadTo/vgerFill, vgerText), but vgerNew and vgerEncode are declared only under __OBJC__ because they take an MTLPixelFormat and an MTLCommandBuffer, so context creation and encoding need Objective-C(++) or Swift. A SwiftUI VgerView wrapper is included. It is not a drop-in for nanovg: names, paint model and path model differ, and nanovg features such as path stroking with joins, scissoring and the nonzero fill rule are missing.
how_it_is_fast: Each primitive becomes one instanced quad, and the fragment shader evaluates the shape's signed distance analytically (SDF, anti-aliased with smoothstep over fwidth), so the CPU does no path tessellation. The CPU only appends primitive records into shared-storage MTLBuffers. A compute pass then computes bounds, and a single instanced draw per layer covers everything, split only when the texture changes. Path fills are cut on the CPU into horizontal slabs (vgerPathScanner), and each slab's quad tests a pixel against only the segments active in that band. The inside test is even-odd: it counts crossings with each segment's chord and flips again inside the region between the curve and its chord, a 'reverse Loop-Blinn' that avoids solving quadratics. Text layouts are cached per string and glyphs go into a CoreGraphics-rasterized atlas.
when_to_use: iOS 14+ or macOS 11+ app whose UI redraws every frame (audio and synth UIs, node editors, plotting) and is CPU-bound in nanovg or CoreGraphics because of path tessellation.
Scenes made mostly of simple shapes (knobs, rounded rects, wires, short quadratic strokes, short text labels), where one instanced draw replaces thousands of tessellated meshes.

You want a small, vendorable MIT renderer with a C drawing API that you can call from C++ or Swift, and you can write a little Objective-C++ or Swift glue for context creation and command-buffer encoding.
Prototyping a GPU UI on Apple hardware that you may later port with the same design via the Rust/wgpu port audulus/vger-rs.
when_not_to_use: Any non-Apple target or headless CPU rendering: it needs Metal, and text depends on CoreText and CoreGraphics; use vger-rs or a CPU rasterizer instead.

SVG or PDF-grade vector output: cubics are approximated by two quadratics ('crude approximation' per vger.h, 'lousy method' per the README), fills are even-odd only, and there are no path strokes with joins, caps or dashes, and vger.h has no clipping, scissor or blend-mode API.

Large or complex paths: vgerQuadTo silently drops segments beyond 1024 per path, and vgerFill gives up (returns false) after 2048 slabs. Per-pixel cost grows with the number of segments active in a slab.

Pixel-exact anti-aliasing: coverage is an SDF smoothstep across about one pixel, not exact area coverage. Open issues report different stroke widths for line and Bezier segments (#7) and propose better AA (#18).
Workloads that need a measured advantage: the only comparison with nanovg is an anecdote, and nothing compares vger with Skia, Rive, Vello or other GPU renderers.

integration.form: Swift Package (Objective-C++ and Metal sources, built as a library; also source-drop into an Xcode project)
integration.dependencies: Apple frameworks only (Metal, MetalKit, CoreText, CoreGraphics); bundles stb_rect_pack; the test target alone depends on wtholliday/MetalNanoVG (branch spm)
integration.min_toolchain: Swift tools 5.9 and C++20 (Package.swift); Xcode with the Metal compiler. Command-line `swift build` fails ('Bundle has no member module', missing default.metallib), open issue #15.
integration.platforms: macOS 11+ and iOS 14+ on Metal GPUs only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. A vgerContext is a mutable struct (transform stack, path scanner, text cache, scene buffers) with no locking, so use one context per thread.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it replaces nanovg's role as an immediate-mode GPU UI renderer, but the API, paint model and feature set differ (no nonzero fill, joins, dashes or scissor; cubics approximated), so call sites must be rewritten

gotchas: Default is single-buffered: unless you pass VGER_DOUBLE_BUFFER or VGER_TRIPLE_BUFFER to vgerNew, vgerBegin reuses the same shared MTLBuffers the GPU may still be reading (vger.mm), so wait for the previous command buffer to finish or turn buffering on.

Overflow can go unreported: vgerQuadTo ignores segments beyond 1024 per path, and GPUVec::append stops adding primitives once a buffer would exceed 256 MB (vgerScene.h). Check vgerFill's return value and vgerPrimCount.

Lines are stored as degenerate quadratics, and cubics are split into two quadratics with no error control, so SVG-style cubic art can visibly deviate. Text is not affected because glyphs are rasterized into an atlas by CoreGraphics.
Paints are per frame: paint indices from vgerColorPaint and the gradient calls become invalid after the next vgerBegin, and invalid indices make vgerFill return false.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick vger over the Rive Renderer, TGFX or vkvg when the app is Apple-only, the scene uses vger's simple primitive set, and you want a few thousand lines of MIT code with a C API rather than a full engine. Pick those siblings (or Vello) when you need cross-platform GPUs, full path semantics or published comparative numbers. It is not comparable to the CPU rasterizers in this category (Blend2D, AGG, Blaze, tiny-skia), which produce exact-coverage pixels without a GPU.
verified_claims_summary: The only number is the author's README anecdote: in the Audulus UI on an unnamed 120 Hz iPad, vger holds 120 fps while nanovg (which nanovg build, presumably Metal, is not stated) drops to 30 fps. The author attributes this to CPU-side tessellation in nanovg. 120 fps is the display cap, so vger's real headroom and the GPU cost are unknown, and there is no scene description, compiler or frame-time data. The commented-out testNanovgPerf in Tests/vgerTests/vgerTests.mm would not be a like-for-like check either. It calls a stale API that no longer exists (vgerColorPaint without a context, a vgerPrim aggregate), strokes 5.12 px wide where testBezierPerf strokes 1 px, and does not wait for nanovg's GPU work, while the vger test waits with waitUntilCompleted and also times its rand() calls.
status_note: Active (commits through 2026-06-08, including a layer-specific encode API, clipped stroke prims and pixel-diff tests) and MIT-licensed (the header carries a zlib-style notice). It ships in the Audulus app, so it is copyable for Apple-only projects, but it is a single-maintainer library with 10 open issues.
